title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
titleOriginal: 神奈川沖浪裏 · The Great Wave
medium: Colour woodblock print, from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
creditLine: Impression held in the Department of Asia
labelText: Three fishing boats are caught in the trough of a wave whose claw of foam hangs over them, and behind it — small, snow-capped, perfectly still — stands Mount Fuji. Hokusai was in his seventies and had been drawing for sixty years. The blue is Prussian blue, a European pigment newly cheap in Japan, and the print's entire modern life begins with it. Thousands of impressions were pulled; this is one of them.
extendedNote:
It is not a painting and never was. Hokusai drew the design; a block-cutter destroyed the drawing in the act of carving it into cherry wood; a printer inked and pulled each impression by hand, one colour block at a time. The image exists in the plural, which is exactly why it travelled. It sold for about the price of a bowl of noodles.

The composition works by a single reversal: the wave is the mountain. Its crest occupies the place a peak would occupy, and the real Fuji is demoted to a small white triangle in the trough, so that a thing which lasts an instant is given the shape of the thing that lasts forever. The boats are oshiokuri-bune, fast craft that carried live fish to Edo, and the men in them are not drowning — they are ducking, in the practised way of people who do this every day. Prussian blue is the other half of the story: an imported synthetic pigment, arriving through the one Dutch trading post Japan allowed, which made possible a print built almost entirely out of blue.

regions.label: The claw of foam
regions.text: The crest breaks into fingers that reach over the boats — a shape Hokusai arrived at over decades of drawing water, and one that photography would later confirm as roughly what a breaking wave actually does. It also puts the wave in the compositional position of a mountain peak, which is the print's central joke and its central idea.

regions.label: Mount Fuji
regions.text: The sacred mountain, the subject of the whole series of thirty-six views, is here reduced to a small white triangle sitting in the trough, so far away that a wave can cover it. The permanent thing is made small and the momentary thing is made enormous. Every other print in the series argues the opposite.

regions.label: The boats
regions.text: Three oshiokuri-bune, the fast, narrow craft that raced live fish into Edo. There are eight rowers to a boat and they are not flailing — they are crouched flat along the thwarts in the practised posture of men who have met this before and expect to meet it again tomorrow.

title: Nebamun Hunting in the Marshes
labelText: Nebamun, a middling accountant of grain at the temple of Amun, stands in a papyrus skiff throwing a stick at wildfowl, his wife behind him in a pleated gown and his daughter crouched at his feet. A tawny cat — gilded eye, three birds in its claws and teeth — hunts alongside him. The marsh is a solid thicket of papyrus and the water below is full of fish drawn as though seen from directly above. It is a painting of an afterlife that looks exactly like a good day.
extendedNote:
The fragment comes from the walls of a small tomb-chapel at Thebes, hacked out in the 1820s by an agent working for the British consul; the tomb itself was never recorded and has not been found since, so these fragments are all that survive of it. They are among the finest painted surfaces to come out of Egypt.

Egyptian painting is often described as rigid, and the composition here is indeed governed by convention: Nebamun is larger than everyone else because he matters more, shown with his head in profile and his shoulders square on, and the register lines organise the world. But look at what happens inside the rules. The birds rising out of the papyrus are painted with an ornithologist's accuracy, species by species. The cat's eye is gilded — the only gold leaf on the wall — and it is looking directly out at you. And the whole scene is a pun: the words for throwing-stick, for the papyrus thicket and for the act of hunting all carry a second sense of creation and rebirth, so the picture of a man enjoying himself is also a diagram of resurrection.

title: The Admonitions Scroll
titleOriginal: 女史箴圖 · Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies
medium: Ink and colour on silk handscroll
dimensions: 24.4 × 343.8 cm — shown here as a section
labelText: One of the earliest Chinese paintings to survive in any form: nine scenes illustrating a third-century text of instruction for palace women, painted in fine line and thin colour on silk. A handscroll is not meant to be hung. It is opened an arm's width at a time, read right to left, and rolled shut behind you — so the picture is experienced as duration rather than as a single view. The section shown here is one of those arm's-widths.
extendedNote:
The scroll is almost certainly a Tang copy of a lost original attributed to Gu Kaizhi, one of the first Chinese painters known by name. That layering is normal in Chinese painting, where copying a master was scholarship rather than forgery, and where the copy carries the original forward when the original perishes.

Its surface is a record of everyone who ever owned it. Emperor Huizong wrote on it in the twelfth century; the Qianlong Emperor added an orchid he painted himself and a great many seals; collectors stamped their marks in red across the silk for a thousand years. It left the Summer Palace during the looting of 1900 and was sold to the British Museum for twenty-five pounds by a cavalry officer who thought the jade toggle was the valuable part. The painting itself is deliberately plain in technique — even, wire-thin outline, colour laid inside it like a wash — because the point of the images is the text they carry, which advises court women that beauty without virtue is a danger and that no one, however favoured, is safe.

title: Mummy Portrait of a Young Man
medium: Encaustic (pigment in hot wax) on limewood panel
labelText: A young man looks out with dark, wide, slightly asymmetrical eyes, a shadow of beard on his jaw, his hair painted in short hooked strokes. The panel was made to be bound into the wrappings of his mummy over his face. It is Roman portraiture — the naturalism, the haircut, the fashion — doing an Egyptian funerary job, and the result is the most direct eye contact anyone makes across two thousand years.
extendedNote:
Several hundred of these panels survive, most from the Fayum basin south-west of Cairo, painted between the first and third centuries AD for a population that was Egyptian, Greek and Roman at once. The technique is encaustic: pigment suspended in hot beeswax, laid on with a brush and a heated metal tool, which sets hard and keeps its colour with almost no fading. That is why the flesh still looks wet.

What startles is not the realism but the specificity. These are individuals — a broken nose, a squint, a mole, an unfashionable beard — and they were painted for people who knew them. Some panels show signs of having hung in a house for years before burial. Nothing else from the ancient world looks back this way; Roman marble portraits are idealised, Egyptian funerary masks are schematic, and these are neither. When the panels began to appear in European collections in the nineteenth century they were treated as archaeology. It took modern painters — who recognised the brushwork immediately — to argue that they were also among the finest portraits ever made.

title: The Geese of Meidum
titleOriginal: From the tomb-chapel of Nefermaat and Itet
creditLine: The original panel is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo; British Museum holdings are 19th-century facsimile copies
labelText: Six geese feed along a strip of ground, three walking left and three walking right, in three pairs of matched species. They are four and a half thousand years old and painted with enough ornithological precision that modern specialists argue about which species they are — and whether one of them ever lived in Egypt at all. Nothing in the panel is stylised except the arrangement, which is perfectly symmetrical.
extendedNote:
A note on where it is: the panel itself was lifted from the tomb-chapel of Nefermaat and his wife Itet at Meidum in the 1870s and has been in Cairo ever since. What the British Museum holds are nineteenth-century facsimiles, made when copying tomb paintings by hand was the only way to bring them to a European audience. Those copies are now historical objects in their own right, and several of the tombs they record have since been destroyed.

The painting technique is unusual for its date: pigment laid into a fine plaster ground rather than the paste-filled incisions Nefermaat's chapel uses elsewhere, which is probably why the colour has held. The composition is arranged for balance — a mirrored pair at each end, a grazing pair at the centre — and within that scheme every bird is observed. White-fronted geese, bean geese, and a pair of red-breasted geese, a species that does not appear in Egypt today and may never have; some scholars take that as evidence of a wider ancient range, and others as evidence that Egyptian painters worked from pattern books as well as from life.

title: Portrait of a Lady
titleOriginal: From the album of White's American watercolours
labelText: John White sailed to Roanoke as the expedition's artist and came back with a body of watercolours that is the earliest European eyewitness record of the peoples, plants and animals of the American east coast. The drawings are quiet, exact and unrhetorical: a standing figure, a fish, a crab, a dance, all set on blank paper with no background at all. This sheet belongs to that album, kept together and later engraved for print, which is how most of Europe first saw America.
extendedNote:
White made three Atlantic crossings and was governor of the second Roanoke colony — the one that vanished. He left for supplies in 1587 and was kept in England by the Armada; when he finally got back in 1590 the settlement, which included his daughter and his granddaughter Virginia Dare, was empty. He never found them, and he never went back.

The watercolours survive because they were copied. Theodor de Bry engraved them in 1590 for a Latin, French, German and English edition of Thomas Harriot's report on Virginia, and in the engraving the figures acquired classical poses and European musculature that White had not given them. White's own sheets are plainer and far better: bodies drawn as observed, tattoo patterns and hair recorded as fact, no allegory, no landscape, nothing arranged. They are also, unavoidably, reconnaissance — a colonising expedition's inventory of a place and its people — and both things are true of them at once.

title: Studies of Birds
labelText: Schouman painted birds from life, in the menageries of Dutch collectors and stadholders, at a moment when live exotic species were arriving in the Netherlands by the shipload and nobody yet knew what most of them were. The results are watercolours of extraordinary delicacy — plumage built up in translucent washes with the paper left bare for the highlights — and they are also, quietly, a record of the reach of the Dutch trading empire.
extendedNote:
He was a decorative painter by trade, producing painted wall-hangings for houses in Dordrecht and The Hague, and the bird studies began as reference material. They outlasted the wallpaper. Schouman worked in the menagerie at Het Kleine Loo and in private collections, drawing from the living animal rather than from skins, which is why his birds stand and grip and look about instead of lying flat like specimens.

Watercolour was the right medium and an unusual choice for the period. Layered thinly, it does what oil cannot easily do with feathers: hold the translucency of a wing edge and the soft dry mass of a breast in the same passage. The technical interest is inseparable from the history — a cockatoo in a Dutch garden in 1760 arrived on a company ship from the far side of the world, and Schouman's careful, affectionate, entirely unsentimental drawings are among the best evidence of what those animals looked like before most of them died in the winter.

title: The Rhinoceros
labelText: Dürer never saw a rhinoceros. One had arrived in Lisbon in 1515, the first in Europe since the Roman empire, and a sketch and a written description travelled north to Nuremberg. From those he cut this: armour-plated, riveted, scaled at the shoulder, with a small twisted horn on its back that no rhinoceros has ever had. It is wrong, and it was believed. For two hundred and fifty years European schoolbooks drew the rhinoceros from this woodcut rather than from the animal.
extendedNote:
The block is cut with the confidence of something observed. Dürer gives the hide the logic of plate armour — gorget, pauldron, tasset — because armour was the closest thing in his workshop's visual vocabulary to a skin arranged in overlapping folds. The engraved-looking texture that covers the legs is a shorthand for reptile scale, and the whole animal is drawn standing on a shallow strip of ground with no landscape at all behind it, so that nothing competes with the description.

The text block above it repeats what Dürer had been told: the date of the animal's arrival, its Indian origin, its supposed enmity with the elephant. It is a news report as much as a picture, and it sold in that spirit — impressions were still being pulled from the block in the eighteenth century. The British Museum's impression comes from the first edition, before the block cracked.

title: Painted Banner from Cave 17, Dunhuang
labelText: In 1900 a Daoist caretaker at the Mogao caves near Dunhuang broke through a plastered wall into a small chamber packed floor to ceiling with manuscripts, silk paintings and banners, sealed for roughly nine hundred years. This banner is one of them: a bodhisattva painted on silk in mineral pigment and ink, made as a votive object to hang in a cave shrine on the edge of the Taklamakan desert.
extendedNote:
Cave 17 held perhaps fifty thousand items — Buddhist sutras in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Sogdian, Uyghur and Khotanese; contracts; a printed Diamond Sutra of 868 that is the earliest dated printed book in existence; and several hundred paintings on silk, hemp and paper. Why it was sealed is still unsettled: an evacuation ahead of an invasion, or a sacred waste deposit for texts too holy to destroy.

Aurel Stein reached the site in 1907 and left with several thousand items for a fraction of what they were worth; Paul Pelliot followed a year later, and the contents of the cave are now divided between London, Paris, Beijing, Delhi and St Petersburg. The paintings themselves are provincial in the best sense — made on a trade route where Chinese, Indian, Tibetan and Central Asian conventions met, by workshops rather than court masters, in a palette of malachite, azurite, cinnabar and gold. The line is fluent and repetitive, the way work is when the same figure has been painted a thousand times, and the silk has kept its colour because it spent nine centuries in the dark.

title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
titleOriginal: 大はしあたけの夕立 · Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi
medium: Colour woodblock print, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
labelText: Rain drawn as line. The downpour is cut into the block as two crossing sets of fine parallel strokes, laid at slightly different angles so the shower has depth, and the figures on the bridge hurry under it with their backs bent and their umbrellas tipped forward. The far bank at Atake has already dissolved into a flat grey band. Nothing in the picture is dramatic except the weather, and the weather is only straight lines.
extendedNote:
The bridge cuts the sheet on a diagonal from lower left to upper right, and everything else is arranged against it: the raft below, the dark water, the vertical rain. Hiroshige uses the bokashi gradation the Edo printers had perfected — ink wiped from the block by hand before each impression — so the river darkens toward the bottom edge and the sky darkens toward the top, and the lit band across the middle is where the whole composition breathes.

Van Gogh copied it in oil in 1887, squaring it up and surrounding it with a border of invented Japanese characters. He could not reproduce the rain: what is a single confident cut in the woodblock became, in paint, a thicket of brushstrokes. The print is the argument for the medium — a shower rendered by a knife in cherrywood, printed identically several thousand times.
